Chapter 9: When to Seek Help—Navigating Systems and Support.
There are times when trusting your gut and taking action just aren’t enough. Sometimes, the threat feels overwhelming, or the situation is so tangled that trying to handle it alone becomes impossible. That’s when knowing how—and when—to reach out for help really becomes essential.
Imagine someone stuck in a tough relationship, where their boundaries keep getting crossed and threats hang in the air. Friends might offer advice, but the fear of things getting worse is real. Maybe they ask themselves, “Am I overreacting? Will anyone actually believe me?” Taking that step to reach out for help isn’t easy. It means being vulnerable, opening yourself up to judgment, and stepping into the unknown.
Here’s something to know: systems like the police, the courts, or counselors—they can be both a lifeline and, sometimes, a source of frustration. Not every report is taken seriously. Not every threat leads to immediate action. But reaching out is still crucial. It creates a record, brings others into your corner, and opens the door to resources you might need.
There are ways to make this process a bit easier. For example, start documenting what’s happening—save threatening messages, jot down incidents, and keep a record. These details can help you build your case if you ever need to. And don’t forget about support from trusted friends, family, or professionals. Sometimes, just knowing someone else is aware can make it a little less frightening to take action.
Remember, help can look different for everyone. Maybe it’s a neighbor who keeps an eye out, a coworker who offers you a ride, or that friend who listens without any judgment. Other times, it’s a shelter, a hotline, or a legal advocate stepping in to help. The main thing is, you don’t have to face danger alone.
A lot of people hold back from asking for help because they worry about being seen as weak, dramatic, or ungrateful. But here’s the truth: reaching out for support is actually a sign of strength. It means you recognize that your safety matters, and that you deserve to feel secure.
Navigating these systems isn’t always easy, but it’s worth it. The more people speak up, the more likely it is that others will be helped, too. The gift of fear is about more than just your own safety—it’s about building a world where we all look out for each other.
